title: HTML: The Structure of the Web
description: Learn what HTML is for, build the minimal html/head/body skeleton every page needs, and understand element nesting as parent/child relationships.

objectives.statement: Explain what HTML is for: describing structure and meaning, not visual styling.
Build a basic HTML document containing html, head, and body, including a heading and a paragraph.
Identify an HTML element in a short snippet and name the parent/child relationship in a small nested structure.

content.title: HTML: The Structure of the Web
content.hook: Every webpage you've ever visited is built on the same skeleton. Once you can see that skeleton, you can build one yourself.
content.context: This is the first hands-on HTML lesson in the module — everything after this builds on the html/head/body structure introduced here.
goals: Build a minimal valid HTML document
Identify elements and nesting in a short snippet

content.title: HTML Describes Structure, Not Appearance
content.text: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes the structure and meaning of content on a page — headings, paragraphs, lists, images — not how that content looks. How things look is CSS's job, which comes later. Every HTML document needs a minimal skeleton: an <html> element as the root, a <head> containing metadata about the document (like its title), and a <body> containing everything the user actually sees. Inside the body, elements can contain other elements — this is called nesting, and it creates a parent/child relationship: the containing element is the parent, and the elements inside it are children.

content.keyTakeaway: html > head + body is the skeleton every page starts from; everything else nests inside body.

content.prompt: Build a minimal valid HTML document with a heading that says "My First Page" and a paragraph that says "I'm learning HTML."

feedback.correct: That's a complete, valid HTML skeleton with real content in it.
feedback.incorrect: Check that you have html, head, and body, plus an h1 and a p with the right text.

content.title: What You Should Take Away
takeaways: HTML describes structure and meaning, not visual appearance — that's CSS's job.
Every document needs the html > head + body skeleton.
Elements can nest inside other elements, forming parent/child relationships.
